name: Sara Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Sara, thank you for joining me. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group. We aren't linked to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you actually think. Can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on what the company calls the grid upgrade crew, out of the Westfield depot. We put in the new kit: reclosers, which are automatic switches that cut the power for a second when a branch brushes the line and then try again, plus line sensors and connections for big battery sites and car chargers. I still climb and work from the bucket like anyone, but I'm also the one with the laptop, setting up the reclosers so they talk to the control room.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you end up being the laptop person?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I just like it. I use AI every day, to read wiring specs, to write the little settings files, to check my maths at ten at night. The older guys call me the help desk, which is fine. Outside work I co-own a duplex with my brother Nico, who's an electrician, and we rent the other half to a young couple. With that and the savings I'm comfortable, which means I can take a few risks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, it's a good tool, not magic, which is what I already think. I'd probably post a few of my favourite ways to use it for line work, because some of them really do save time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, nothing changes. The grid still needs upgrading, there are more chargers and batteries every year, and that's work for decades. AI is just my assistant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. Keep learning the new kit, keep using the tools, keep the duplex rented. Maybe Nico and I buy a second place in a few years if prices stay sensible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pretty content with that world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you miss, if AI stayed this modest?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing much. I use it as a very patient colleague who knows every manual. If that's all it ever is, I'm happy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the rental side change at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Ana and Ben pay rent on time, the boiler's new, so it's boring in a good way. Boring rentals are the best kind.

S0.say: She'd say AI is a good tool rather than magic, which is what she already believes. She might post her favourite ways of using it in line work.
S0.think: She thinks nothing changes for her, because grid upgrades for chargers and batteries mean decades of work. AI stays her assistant.
S0.do: Keeps learning new equipment, keeps using AI tools and keeps the duplex rented. Considers buying a second property with her brother in a few years.
S0.quote: I use it as a very patient colleague who knows every manual.
S0.fieldNote: Sara is the tech person on her crew and already uses AI daily without hype. Her security comes from both her skills and a rental property she co-owns with her brother. She sees a long runway of grid upgrade work regardless of AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good time to be the person who understands both the wires and the software. At work I'd tell people to learn the tools now, while it's optional. I'd probably run a little lunchtime session if the depot let me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this picture helps me. The grid gets smarter, and someone has to install the smart bits and set them up. That's literally my job already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the grid automation technician course the company offers, so I'm officially qualified for what I already do unofficially. I'd use AI more for fault analysis. And Nico and I would probably buy that second place sooner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any risk to you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some of the inspection and design work might move to software, and maybe fewer people on the planning side. I'm on the doing side, so I'd be fine. I'd keep an eye on it though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you help the rest of your crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Show them shortcuts, mostly. Nobody's going to learn from a two-hundred-page manual, but they'll learn from me showing them on my phone over a sandwich.

S1.say: She'd say it's a good time to understand both wires and software, and urge colleagues to learn the tools while it's optional. She'd offer lunchtime sessions at the depot.
S1.think: She thinks this picture helps her, because a smarter grid needs people to install and set up the smart equipment, which is already her job.
S1.do: Takes the company's grid automation technician course to formalise what she already does and uses AI more for fault analysis. Buys a second property with her brother sooner.
S1.quote: Nobody's going to learn from a two-hundred-page manual, but they'll learn from me showing them on my phone over a sandwich.
S1.fieldNote: She sees steady change as good for her and moves straight to formalising her skills. She is generous with colleagues and thinks about how people actually learn. Her investment plans speed up rather than slow down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to need an insane amount of electricity. Every one of those AI systems and robots runs on power, and someone has to build the lines to the data centres. I'd be telling everyone at the depot that the next two years are a gold rush for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's a boom and then a cliff. For two years, people like me are worth a fortune, connecting data centres and robot factories. After that, robots build the lines too, and I don't know what I'd do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go contract, straight away, on the big data centre connection projects, because they'd pay double. Every extra bit would go into savings and maybe a share of a second property. I'd want to come out of those two years with as much as possible put away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Excited and uneasy at once, like being on a train that's going too fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You don't seem as worried as I'd expect. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the next two years would be good for me, and I've got property and savings. The bit after is scary, but it's scary for everyone, not just me. I'd rather have money and skills than not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Ana and Ben, your tenants?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the part I hadn't thought about. If they lose their jobs, they can't pay rent, and I'm not going to throw out a young couple in that situation. So the rental isn't as safe as I like to tell myself.

S2.say: She'd say AGI would need enormous amounts of electricity for data centres and robots, making the next two years a gold rush for lineworkers. She'd tell everyone at the depot so.
S2.think: She thinks it would be a boom followed by a cliff: two lucrative years connecting data centres and robot factories, then robots building lines too. She doesn't know what she'd do after.
S2.do: Goes contract straight away on data centre connection projects that pay double, putting every extra amount into savings and possibly a share of a second property. Aims to bank as much as possible in those two years.
S2.feel: Excited and uneasy at once, like a train going too fast.
S2.quote: Every one of those AI systems and robots runs on power, and someone has to build the lines to the data centres.
S2.fieldNote: Sara saw something the card didn't spell out: the electricity demand of AGI could create a short boom for her trade. The follow-up about her tenants exposed a weak spot in her sense of security, and she admitted it honestly. She would make money fast rather than protect what she has.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as the fast one: we're going to be busy. I'd add that people should use the busy years to prepare, not just spend the overtime. That's practical advice, not doom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is enough to build something of my own before the cliff. Not a job, a business. If I own part of the work, I'm not just waiting to be replaced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one, Nico and I would start a small business installing home batteries and car chargers, evenings and weekends at first. I'd use AI for quoting and scheduling, and if robots for install work came along, I'd buy one rather than compete with it. I'd keep my day job for the steady pay until the business could stand up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Busy and a bit nervous, but in a good way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years let you do that two doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is grab the money. Five years is build something. That's the difference for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Like you said with the fast one, there's a cliff at the end. What's your plan for the cliff?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Own the robots, not be the robot. If a machine can install a charger, I'd want it to be my machine, with my name on the van. That's the only plan that makes sense to me.

S3.say: She'd say lineworkers would be busy and should use those years to prepare rather than spend the overtime. She'd frame it as practical advice, not doom.
S3.think: She thinks five years is enough to build a business of her own before the cliff. If she owns part of the work, she isn't just waiting to be replaced.
S3.do: Starts a home battery and car charger installation business with her brother in the first year, evenings and weekends at first, using AI for quoting and scheduling. Plans to buy install robots rather than compete with them and keeps her day job until the business can stand alone.
S3.feel: Mostly calm, busy and a little nervous in a good way.
S3.quote: Own the robots, not be the robot.
S3.fieldNote: The extra three years shift her from grabbing money to building ownership. Her plan is specific and staged, with her brother as partner and her day job as a safety net. She's pragmatic rather than ideological about who wins and loses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so use it. Learn the tools, save, build something. I'd be the annoying one at the depot saying that every week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is great for me. I'd grow the business slowly, keep the day job longer, and be thirty-seven with a company and two properties, hopefully. I'm not worried for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still start the business with Nico, maybe a year or two later and with less rush. I'd keep investing and do the automation course too. And I'd keep using every new tool the week it comes out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Honestly, a bit optimistic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about ten years that worries you more than five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only that people would waste it. Ten years sounds like forever, and I've seen how slowly the depot moves. Some of the guys would still be saying it's hype in year nine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want governments to do with the decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Make retraining easy and cheap and fast, and don't strangle small businesses with paperwork. I don't need much else. Other people would need more help than me, and I'd support that.

S4.say: She'd say a decade is a gift and people should learn the tools, save and build something. She'd repeat that weekly at the depot.
S4.think: She thinks ten years is great for her: she'd grow the business slowly, keep her day job longer and hopes to be thirty-seven with a company and two properties. She isn't worried for herself.
S4.do: Starts the business with her brother a year or two later and with less rush, keeps investing and takes the automation course. Adopts each new tool the week it arrives.
S4.quote: Some of the guys would still be saying it's hype in year nine.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Sara is optimistic about her own future and her worry turns to slower colleagues. Her policy asks are modest and pragmatic: fast, cheap retraining and less paperwork for small businesses, with support for others who need more. She's consistent across speeds in wanting ownership.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, but not for the reason people think. The first two years would be good for me. It's the cliff after, and the tenants, and everyone else around me with no time to adjust. What would help is easy, fast retraining and support for people who can't jump like I can.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the electricity. Everyone talks about robots taking jobs, nobody talks about who builds the power for them. For a while that's us.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Thank you. That's everything I needed.

headlineQuote: Everyone talks about robots taking jobs, nobody talks about who builds the power for them.
portrait: Sara Torres is a 27-year-old lineworker on a grid upgrade crew, installing reclosers, sensors and battery connections and setting them up from her laptop. She co-owns a rented duplex with her electrician brother Nico, has solid savings and uses AI every day as a patient colleague. She is calm or pleased through most pictures and expects AGI to bring a short boom for lineworkers building power to data centres. A two-year warning leaves her uneasy about the cliff after the boom and about her tenants, while five or ten years lead her to start a battery and charger business with her brother. Her motto is to own the robots, not be the robot.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, not for the first two years but for the cliff after, her tenants and the people around her with no time to adjust.
whatWouldHelp: Easy, fast retraining and support for people who can't change course as quickly as she can.
